How to Play Azul: Rules and How to Win

2026-10-19

How to play Azul: take every tile of one color from a factory, or from the middle of the table, and stack them onto a single row of your board. When that row fills up, one tile hops over to the wall and scores. Most points when the game ends wins. That is the whole loop, and it teaches in about two minutes.

Then you play your first real game and lose by 25 points without knowing where they went. I did exactly that four nights in a row. The rules are simple and the scoring is simple. What nobody tells you on the first night is the part that actually decides games: the tiles you leave behind are a move too.

I have played Azul well over 50 times, on a shelf that also holds its sequels, and the pattern never changes. Beginners lose to the floor line, not to better tile pickers. So here are the rules in the order they click, then the one habit that flips a 25-point gap.

What Is in the Box

The box holds 100 tiles, 20 in each of five colors: blue, yellow, red, black, and white. Nine cardboard factory discs. Four double-sided player boards. One cloth bag, four scoring markers, and one starting player marker.

The player board is where all the thinking happens, so look at it once before you read the rules. The left half is five pattern lines, and they hold 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 tiles. The right half is the wall, a 5x5 grid where every row and every column holds each color exactly once. That diagonal pattern is fixed and printed on the board. You never choose where a tile lands on the wall.

Notice what this means. You do not build a wall in Azul, you fill rows and hope the wall lines up. The board's diagonal is the puzzle, and it is the reason two players can hold the same tiles and score 20 points apart.

Setup in Two Minutes

Give everyone a board, colored side up, and a scoring marker on zero. Put the factory discs in a circle around the middle of the table. The count depends on your group: 5 discs for two players, 7 for three, 9 for four.

Fill the bag with all 100 tiles. Then draw 4 tiles at random for each factory disc. The middle of the table starts empty, and it stays empty for exactly one turn.

For the first player, the rulebook has a joke that has survived every printing: the player who most recently visited Portugal goes first. If nobody has been to Portugal, the youngest player starts. Grab the starting marker, take the first turn, and you are playing.

Your Turn: One Color, One Row

On your turn you do one of two things. Take all the tiles of a single color from one factory disc, and then slide every leftover tile from that disc into the middle of the table. Or take all the tiles of a single color from the middle of the table, where everyone's leftovers pile up.

Then all the tiles you picked go onto exactly one pattern line, and they all have to be the same color. A line that already holds blue accepts more blue and nothing else. If the line only has two spaces left and you picked three tiles, the third one goes to your floor line below the board.

There is one restriction that shows up in round two and not round one. You cannot start a new color in a pattern line if that same row of your wall already holds that color. Learn this early. I have watched a full table try to add red to a row that had red on the wall, and the rulebook has to be opened.

Play continues clockwise until every factory disc and the middle of the table are empty. That is one round. A game usually runs five to seven of them.

The Leftover Rule: What You Leave Is a Move

This is the part that decides most games, and it hides in plain sight. When you take from a factory, the tiles you did not want do not disappear. They move to the center, where any player can scoop them up on their next turn. Nothing is thrown away. Every pick you make is also a gift.

Here is the key insight, and it took me about 20 games to feel it: count the pile you hand to the table before you count the pile you take. A disc with 3 whites and 1 black is not a white pile. It is a white pile that drops a black tile in the middle for whoever is building black.

Pay attention to this number: the center. On most turns in the middle of a game, the middle of the table holds more tiles than any single disc, because six or eight turns have already leaked into it. New players ignore it. Experienced players treat it as the main shop.

Two habits fall out of this. First, when the middle is fat and you can actually use what is in it, take from the middle. Second, when you empty a disc, look at what is left before you commit, and if the leftovers feed the player on your left, look for a different pick.

This Is Where It Gets Interesting

For my first few months I played Azul like a shopper. Find the biggest pile of one color, grab it, feel great about it. Three tiles in my hand is better than one, every time.

Then I started tracking why I kept losing to the same friend. Not once did she take the biggest pile. She took one tile from a full factory more often than not, and then she watched what dropped into the middle. In one game she took exactly 12 tiles across five rounds and still finished on 61 points. I took 19 and finished on 43.

Here is the contradiction. Every beginner guide says grab the biggest pile, and the biggest pile is usually the trap. Taking four tiles means three are excess if your line is short, and excess is a floor line penalty. Taking one tile costs you nothing and dumps three into the middle for everyone. Small picks are not careful play. They are aggressive play, and it took me a long time to see it.

The Floor Line: Where First Games Are Lost

Under every board is a floor line with seven spaces. Tiles that do not fit anywhere go there, filling left to right, and they sting at the end of the round. The penalties read -1, -1, -2, -2, -2, -3, -3. Fill all seven and you lose 14 points in a single round.

Fourteen points is a third of a good game. And it is not rare: beginners fill three or four spaces in round one, and the game is effectively over before the wall makes sense. My worst single round was a 9-point hit, and I remember the exact tile: a red I took because it was sitting alone and looked lonely.

The starting player marker works the same way. Whoever first takes tiles from the middle takes the marker, drops it on the leftmost free floor space, and pays a point for it. In exchange, they go first next round. Early in the game that trade is bad. In the last round it is often the best move on the table.

How a Round Ends and How You Score

When the discs and the middle are empty, everyone scores at the same time. Go down your pattern lines from the top. Every line that is completely full sends its rightmost tile to the wall, onto the space matching that color, and scores immediately.

The scoring rule for a placed tile is the one thing worth memorizing. A lonely tile is 1 point. A tile with neighbors scores 1 point for itself plus 1 for each tile linked to it in a straight line, horizontally and vertically counted separately. So a tile that completes a row of 3 and also touches a column of 2 scores 3 plus 2 for 5 points.

Then subtract your floor line. Your score can never drop below zero, which is a small mercy for round one disasters.

The game ends after the round in which any player completes a horizontal line of five on their wall. Then you add the bonuses, and these are where games flip: 2 points for every complete row, 7 points for every complete column, and 10 points for every color where all five of your wall tiles match. A player who looked 8 points ahead on the track can lose to a finished column, because that column is worth more than three rows.

Ties go to the player with more complete horizontal lines. I have never seen it come to a shared win.

Three Habits That Turn Losses Around

Nothing here needs a spreadsheet. It needs one game of paying attention.

Build the middle, then shop in it. The center is your best store after round two. When you can use what is there, take from the center and let the factories keep leaking.

Finish a short line early. The first two rows take 3 tiles total and give you two wall tiles to build chains around. Players who hoard big lines for later spend the whole game with 3 points on the board.

Read your neighbor's open rows. Their wall shows you which colors they still need. If the disc has the exact color their next row wants and you can take something else, take something else. Denial costs you nothing and it is the quiet half of the game.

Which Azul Should You Buy

So now you know the rules. The next question is which box, because Azul is a whole family of games now and they are not equally good at everything. Prices below are what I saw the week I checked, and they bounce with every Amazon sale.

Start with Azul, the 2017 original by Michael Kiesling. It runs about $32, seats 2 to 4, and it is the version every review and every shelf reference means. Between $28 and $35 is a normal price. The full stats live on my Azul page.

One honest warning. Two-player Azul is a knife. With only two people the middle of the table is thinner, denial is stronger, and an early floor line is nearly unrecoverable. If you mostly play with one other person, read the next paragraph instead.

Azul: Summer Pavilion is the one I hand to couples. It keeps the same pick and place bones, then adds wild tiles and a more forgiving middle, so a bad round is a scratch instead of a knockout. It usually sits around $35 to $40. New to the shelf and already the game my two-player nights reach for, and it has a page of its own at Azul: Summer Pavilion.

One honest warning. The wild tiles make the first game feel easier than it is, and the scoring board has more moving parts than the original. Teach it after you have played the base game once, not before.

Azul: Stained Glass of Sintra is the mean one, released in 2018. It adds a moving glazier pawn and a mechanic that can crush your own finished glass, so the table talk gets personal. Around $30 to $38. It shows up in my roundup of strategy games for groups who find the base game too polite.

One honest warning. It is harder to teach and harder to love quickly. Two of the four people I taught it to asked for the original back the same night.

Azul Mini is the same game in a smaller box with smaller tiles and travel trays that hold everything in place. Usually $18 to $25, and it plays identically. I keep it in a bag for cafe tables that are the size of a laptop.

One honest warning. Small tiles mean small hands only. My group has dropped more than one tile under a table, and the trays are tight enough that you need a moment to set them up.

Azul Duel is the 2025 two-player game, and it is the sharpest of the family. Every kind of tile has a power, the board is tight, and there is no middle-of-the-table truce. It runs about $28 to $35, and if you want the head-to-head depth of the 2-player games list, this belongs on it.

One honest warning. It teaches slower than the original. The rulebook is thin but the tile powers add up, so plan a full first game just for learning.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive 10 plays on a shelf that already holds 40 boxes? Azul passes with room to spare, and it passes for a reason most modern games cannot match: setups take 90 seconds, the rules never need to be reopened after night one, and the same four people get sharper instead of bored. Ten plays in, you stop counting tiles you want and start counting tiles you are leaving. That is the moment the game opens up.

Summer Pavilion earns its spot right next to it, mostly because it plays so well with two. Stained Glass of Sintra is the one box on this list I would sell before the others.

Here is the part that matters. Get the base Azul first, around $32, and put it on the table with the leftover rule already in your head. If your game nights are two people, get Azul: Summer Pavilion instead. Catch the base under $28 or Summer Pavilion under $35 and you have done well, since both move with every sale. If you are still picking a first modern game, my beginner list starts where this one ends, and the full strategy lineup covers what to buy after Azul stops surprising you.
